I can’t bring myself to eat anything with fat or sugar. Just the thought of butter, oil, or sweets makes me anxious—like just one bite will make me gain ten pounds instantly. It’s not that I’m obsessed with germs or food needing to be “just right,” like some people. It’s the fear—the absolute certainty—that eating those foods will ruin my body. I measure everything, cut portions into tiny bits. Sometimes I chew and spit because I can’t stand the idea of calories staying in my system. My daughter says I’m too thin, that I need to eat, but to me, I still feel like I need to lose more. It’s not about being neat or orderly—it’s about staying thin. I’m down to 98 pounds—my husband keeps saying it, my clothes hang off me—but the idea of eating more makes me so anxious. I restrict myself to about 800 calories a day, mostly just steamed vegetables, plain rice, and tea. If I eat anything with fat or sugar, I panic, convinced I’ll gain weight immediately, like just one bite will change everything.  

I weigh myself twice a day and measure everything I eat down to the gram. I’ve even started cutting food into tiny pieces before eating it. It feels like a ritual, but it’s not about cleanliness or control in a general sense—it’s all tied to not getting bigger. My work as an art restorer requires precision, and I used to find comfort in that, but now that need for control bleeds into every meal. I look in the mirror and still see someone who needs to lose more, even when my reflection is almost skeletal. I know people worry, but gaining weight feels like the worst thing that could happen.

I’ve always been particular about routines—part of the job, really. As an auctioneer, you’ve got to be sharp, on time, predictable. But lately, my eating’s gotten… tight. Not that I’m worried, but I’ll have a bite or two at dinner, maybe a cracker earlier, and that’s it. My wife notices, says I’m not myself, but I tell her I’m just not hungry. 

Weight? I don’t track it, but I know I’m thinner. Honestly, the idea of gaining weight unsettles me—a bit like losing control. But it’s not like I’m looking in the mirror all day. I just feel better, clearer, when I stick to strict limits. It’s not about looks. It’s about order.

There are rules I follow with food—how it’s placed, how much, when. If something’s touched another item on the plate, I’ll stop. Sounds silly, I know. But breaking the pattern feels… wrong. Not dangerous, just *off*. My wife thinks I’m scared of food, or of gaining weight. I can’t say I blame her for thinking that. But I don’t feel sick. I feel precise. In control. And if I’m under, well, I’ve never been one to eat much anyway.
D021-D016_h022.question_a:
I’ve always been particular about how I present myself—when you're on stage calling auctions, your image matters. But over the past six months, I’ve had this constant, gnawing fear that if I eat more than a bite or two at a meal, I’ll start gaining weight… and once it starts, I won’t be able to stop. I’m terrified of becoming fat. I know I’ve lost a lot of weight—my suits hang off me now—but my wife keeps worrying, saying I’m too thin, that I look sick. I just don’t see it. I feel in control for the first time in years.

I measure everything—how much food is on the plate, the exact number of chews, the timing of when I can eat. I’ll rearrange my meals, cut food into tiny pieces, line them up—sometimes I feel like I have to do it just right. But it’s all tied to keeping the calories as low as possible. It’s not about cleanliness or rituals—it’s about not gaining weight. My wife thinks I have some kind of compulsion, but it’s not random—it’s focused. If I let go, I’m afraid I’ll lose myself.
D021-D016_h022.question_b:
I’ve always been a talker—being an auctioneer, you have to be. But lately, my voice isn’t the one running the show. It’s this constant noise in my head about food. I stand at the podium, selling tractors and furniture, and all I can think about is whether the sandwich I ate at lunch touched the wrapper in the exact same spot as yesterday. If it didn’t, I feel like something’s wrong, like the day is off, and I have to mentally replay it.

I eat, but only in these strict, tiny rituals—one bite here, one bite there, always the same. It’s not about losing weight. In fact, my wife keeps telling me I need to gain a few pounds, but that’s not why I do it. I’m not scared of getting fat. I actually worry more about *not* doing the rituals. If I don’t prepare my food the same way—same plate, same placement, same sequence—I get this overwhelming dread that something awful will happen, maybe to her. 

It’s exhausting. But skipping the routine? That feels impossible. Like tempting fate. The small eating isn’t about my body—it’s about controlling the thoughts.
